# Nandakovāda Sutta (MN 146 (PTS MN iii 270))

**ID:** MN 146 (PTS MN iii 270)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Nandakovāda Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** Advice from Nandaka
**PTS:** MN iii 270
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nandakovāda Sutta* ("Advice from Nandaka", MN 146) is set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The narrative begins when Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approaches the Buddha accompanied by five hundred nuns to request Dhamma instruction [Anālayo 2010; Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Although the monk Nandaka had previously been avoiding his assigned turn to instruct the nuns, the Buddha specifically directs him to teach them, addressing him with high regard as "brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) [Anālayo 2016; Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. Nandaka structures his discourse as an interactive catechism, explicitly inviting the nuns to engage, respond, and ask for further explanation if needed [Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. He leads them through a detailed examination of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and not-self (*anattā*) across the internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*) and their corresponding types of consciousness [Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Rogell 2003]. To explain how passion binds the faculties, Nandaka presents a sequence of allegories: comparing the external bases to a great tree, and likening the internal and external faculties to the flesh and hide of a cow bound by inner sinews and tendons (representing desire and lust), which are severed by the sharp butcher's knife of noble wisdom [Kuznetsova et al. 2012].

Comparative analysis by Bhikkhu Anālayo highlights that in the Pali version, the Buddha does not directly address or teach Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, unlike several non-Theravāda parallel accounts where he teaches her personally; Anālayo identifies this feature as part of a later redactional tendency toward narrative distancing of nuns within the Theravāda tradition [Anālayo 2010; Anālayo 2011; Anālayo 2016]. Curated parallels include a discourse in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 276 / T 99), Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 68 and 85), Tibetan Kangyur translations (D 3 and D 4106), and a Sarvāstivāda/Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya version (T 1442.30). The sutta is also cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 13.8).

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: SA 276 難陀說法; SHT Sutta 68; SHT Sutta 85; D 4106 སོ་སོར་ཐར་པའི་མདོའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ་འདུལ་བ་ཀུན་ལས་བཏུས་པ (pratimokṣasūtraṭīkāvinayasamuccaya); T 1442.30 根本說一切有部毘奈耶
- Passage-level parallels: d3 འདུལ་བ་རྣམ་པར་འབྱེད་པ། (Bhikṣunī-vinaya-vibhaṅga)
- Mentioned in: Kv 13.8 Asātarāgakathā

**Sources**

- [Anālayo 2010] Bhikkhu Anālayo, 'Attitudes Towards Nuns: A Case Study of the Nandakovāda', Journal of Buddhist Ethics (2010) — Analysis of the opening narrative, Mahāpajāpatī's meeting with the Buddha, absence of garudharma regulations, and Tibetan/Chinese parallels.
- [Anālayo 2011] Bhikkhu Anālayo, 'The Buddha’s Past Life as a Princess in the Ekottarika-āgama' (2011) — Observation on narrative distancing and the Buddha not speaking directly to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī in MN 146.
- [Anālayo 2016] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Foundation History of the Nuns’ Order (2016) — Discussion of narrative distancing of nuns, comparison with parallels, and the use of 'brāhmaṇa' as a term of high regard.
- [Kuznetsova et al. 2012] Irina Kuznetsova, Jonardon Ganeri, Chakravarthi Ram-Prasad, Hindu and Buddhist Ideas in Dialogue: Self and No-Self (2012) — Detailed summary of Nandaka's catechism to the nuns, the 18 dhātus, and the similes of the tree, the cow, and the butcher's knife.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — English title, setting at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, and opening passage details.
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner’s Study Guide (2003) — Characterization of the sutta's doctrinal emphasis on impermanence.
